overview: Anomaly detection in data quality is the automated identification of unexpected deviations in pipeline metrics—row counts, null rates, distinct counts, freshness lag, and statistical distributions—that signal a problem in upstream data or processing logic.

Unlike static threshold rules that only catch known failure modes, statistical and ML-based anomaly detectors learn the 'normal' behavior of a metric over time and flag deviations that no human would have anticipated, catching the unknown-unknowns of data quality.

Modern data observability platforms (Monte Carlo, Anomalo) and open-source tools (Amazon Deequ, Soda, dbt metric history) embed anomaly detection directly into data pipelines, turning silent data corruption into actionable, explainable alerts.

Effective anomaly detection on data quality metrics requires handling seasonality, trend, and cold-start, tuning sensitivity to avoid alert fatigue, and integrating with distribution shift detection to catch not just volume anomalies but also changes in the statistical shape of data.
learningObjectives: Understand and implement statistical anomaly detection methods (z-score, IQR, MAD, rolling windows, EWMA) on time-series data quality metrics.
Apply distribution shift detection techniques (PSI, KS test, histogram comparison) to identify when the statistical character of data has changed.
Contrast static thresholds with dynamic/adaptive anomaly detection, and tune detectors for seasonality, false positives, and alert fatigue.
Design an end-to-end anomaly detection architecture for a production data pipeline using industry tools (Monte Carlo, Anomalo, Soda, Deequ, dbt).
Explain time-series decomposition approaches (STL, Prophet, ARIMA-style) and ML detectors (Isolation Forest) at a level relevant to data engineering.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Anomaly detection in data quality is the application of statistical, time-series, and machine-learning methods to a historical record of pipeline health metrics—row counts, null rates, distinct counts, freshness lag, mean, percentiles, and distribution summaries—to identify observations that deviate significantly from learned baselines, accounting for trend and seasonality, so that data quality incidents are detected automatically without requiring an exhaustive set of hand-written static rules.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Every day your pipeline produces numbers: how many rows loaded, what fraction were null, what the average transaction amount was. Anomaly detection watches those numbers over time and learns what 'normal' looks like, including the fact that Mondays are always busier than Saturdays. When today's number is far outside what history suggests it should be, it raises an alert, even if you never wrote a rule for that specific failure mode. It is the difference between a smoke alarm calibrated to your house versus a list of every possible fire you can imagine.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Early data warehouse monitoring relied entirely on static, hand-maintained thresholds—if row count dropped below 1 million, alert. This approach required engineers to anticipate every failure mode and broke silently whenever data volumes grew or patterns shifted seasonally. The 'data observability' movement, pioneered commercially by Monte Carlo (~2019) and Anomalo, applied the ideas of ML-based anomaly detection (long established in IT infrastructure monitoring via tools like Datadog) to data pipeline metrics. Amazon Deequ (2018, open-sourced from AWS internal tooling) introduced declarative anomaly detection strategies on Spark. Simultaneously, dbt's metric exposure capability and Soda's anomaly checks brought statistical monitoring to SQL-first teams. By the early 2020s, automated, adaptive anomaly detection on data quality metrics had become a standard expectation in mature data platforms.

whyItMatters.business: Silent data quality incidents—a 40% row-count drop, a null spike in a revenue column, a sudden shift in the distribution of a key feature—corrupt dashboards, ML model predictions, and regulatory reports before anyone notices. Automated anomaly detection shrinks mean-time-to-detection from days to minutes, protecting business decisions from bad data.
whyItMatters.engineering: Static rules require an engineer to anticipate every possible failure and update thresholds as data evolves. Anomaly detection adapts automatically to changing volumes, seasonal patterns, and trends, reducing the maintenance burden while covering failure modes that rules would never catch.
whyItMatters.scalability: As the number of monitored tables, columns, and metrics grows to hundreds or thousands, maintaining hand-crafted thresholds per metric is unscalable. Model-based detectors parameterize automatically from history and generalize across any numeric metric time series.
whyItMatters.cost: Every hour of undetected data corruption has downstream costs: wrong decisions, reprocessing of downstream models and reports, stakeholder trust erosion, and SLA breach penalties. Early detection via anomaly alerting cuts remediation cost dramatically.
whyItMatters.reliability: Anomaly detection on data quality metrics is the equivalent of service uptime monitoring for data products. It makes data reliability measurable, alertable, and improvable over time, turning data SLAs from aspirational commitments into operationally enforced guarantees.

coreComponents.name: Metrics History Store
coreComponents.definition: A persistent time-series table or database that records pipeline health metrics (row count, null rate, distinct count, freshness lag, mean, percentiles, distribution summaries) per table, partition, and run timestamp.
coreComponents.purpose: To provide the historical baseline from which anomaly detectors learn normal behavior and against which current observations are compared.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Capture metric values at each pipeline run, partition by table/column/date, retain sufficient history (typically 30-90 days) for seasonal learning, and expose the history efficiently for detector queries.
coreComponents.examples: A `metrics_history` table with columns (table_name, metric_name, partition_date, value, computed_at); Soda Cloud's metric store; Monte Carlo's metrics backend; dbt exposures feeding a metrics mart.

coreComponents.name: Statistical Detector
coreComponents.definition: An algorithm that computes a baseline (mean, standard deviation, IQR, EWMA, or a time-series model) from historical metric values and evaluates whether the current observation is a statistically significant outlier.
coreComponents.purpose: To separate true anomalies from normal variance without requiring hand-tuned absolute thresholds, using adaptive baselines that handle trend and seasonality.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Compute bounds (e.g., mean +/- k*std) from a rolling window of historical values, apply seasonality-aware grouping (e.g., compare only to same-day-of-week history), flag observations outside bounds, and return a severity score.
coreComponents.examples: Z-score detector on a 30-day rolling window of daily row counts; IQR-based detector on null rates; EWMA smoothing for detecting gradual drift; Isolation Forest for multi-dimensional metric anomalies.

coreComponents.name: Distribution Shift Detector
coreComponents.definition: A component that compares the statistical distribution of a column or metric between a reference (baseline) period and a current period, detecting changes in shape, mean, or tail behavior that volume-only metrics would miss.
coreComponents.purpose: To catch data drift—changes in the statistical character of values—which is especially critical for ML feature pipelines where distribution shift degrades model performance.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Compute population stability index (PSI) or run a Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test between baseline and current distributions, bin continuous values into histograms, flag PSI > 0.2 or statistically significant KS p-values as distribution anomalies.
coreComponents.examples: PSI computed between last month's order amount distribution and this month's; scipy KS test comparing a training feature distribution to a serving feature distribution; histogram overlap comparison.

coreComponents.name: Alert and Routing Engine
coreComponents.definition: The component that translates detector outputs (anomaly flags, severity scores, metric values, computed bounds) into actionable notifications routed to the right owners.
coreComponents.purpose: To close the loop between detection and remediation, ensuring the right person receives a clear, actionable alert with enough context to triage the issue quickly.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Deduplicate and suppress noisy alerts, apply severity thresholds before notifying, enrich alerts with context (table lineage, last-good run, failing metric and bound), route by dataset owner, and track alert acknowledgement and resolution.
coreComponents.examples: Slack notification with table name, metric, current value, expected bounds, and link to quarantine rows; PagerDuty escalation for SLA-breaching anomalies; Monte Carlo's lineage-aware incident feed.

internalWorking: At each pipeline run, the anomaly detection system computes a set of metrics for each monitored table or column (row count, null rate, distinct count, mean, p50/p95, freshness lag) and appends them to a metrics history store with the run timestamp and partition date.

The statistical detector queries the history store for the rolling window of past observations (e.g., last 28 same-day-of-week values to handle weekly seasonality) and computes a baseline distribution: typically mean and standard deviation, or median and MAD for robustness to outliers.

Bounds are computed (e.g., mean +/- 3*std for z-score, or Q1 - 1.5*IQR to Q3 + 1.5*IQR for IQR), and the current observation is checked against those bounds; an observation outside the bounds is flagged as anomalous with a severity score proportional to the deviation.

For time-series models (STL decomposition, Prophet, ARIMA-style), the detector fits a trend and seasonality model to the historical metric series, generates a forecast with confidence intervals for the current period, and flags the observation if it falls outside the interval.

Distribution shift detectors compare column-level histograms or CDFs between a baseline window and the current batch using PSI or the KS statistic; results above a threshold (PSI > 0.2, KS p-value < 0.05) trigger a distribution anomaly alert distinct from volume or freshness alerts.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Pipeline run -> Compute metrics (row count, null rates, distinct counts, freshness, distribution summaries) -> Append to metrics_history store -> Statistical detector queries rolling window -> Compute baseline bounds (z-score / IQR / EWMA / Prophet) -> Compare current observation -> Anomalous? -> Yes: enrich alert (table, metric, value, bounds, lineage) -> Route to owner (Slack / PagerDuty) -> Incident triage + remediation | No: log clean run -> Dashboard updates
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A daily orders pipeline completes its load to staging; a post-load metric computation step counts rows (142,000), computes null_rate for order_id (0.002), distinct customer count (38,400), and freshness lag (1.2 hours), then appends all four metrics to the metrics_history table alongside today's date and partition.

2. The z-score anomaly detector queries the last 28 same-day-of-week row-count values from metrics_history (e.g., all Tuesdays for the last 28 weeks), computes mean=148,500 and std=4,200, and derives bounds [135,900, 161,100]; today's 142,000 falls within bounds so no alert fires.

3. The null_rate detector finds today's 0.002 within the expected range; however, the distinct customer count of 38,400 versus a rolling mean of 51,200 (std=2,100) produces a z-score of -6.1, well outside the threshold of +/-3, flagging a severe anomaly.

4. The PSI distribution detector compares the binned order_amount distribution against last month's baseline and computes PSI=0.31, exceeding the 0.2 threshold and flagging a significant distribution shift in order amounts.

5. The alert engine deduplicates the two anomalies (distinct count and distribution shift), enriches each with table lineage showing downstream dashboards and the revenue ML model, and routes Slack notifications to the orders pipeline owner with current values, expected bounds, and a link to investigate.

keyTerminology.meaning: A standardized measure of how many standard deviations an observation is from the mean of a reference distribution: z = (x - mean) / std. Observations with |z| > 3 are conventionally flagged as anomalous.
keyTerminology.importance: The simplest and most widely used anomaly score for univariate metric time series; easy to implement and explain, but sensitive to non-Gaussian distributions and influenced by outliers in the reference window.

keyTerminology.meaning: The range between the 25th percentile (Q1) and 75th percentile (Q3) of a distribution. Anomaly bounds are set at Q1 - 1.5*IQR (lower) and Q3 + 1.5*IQR (upper), matching Tukey's fences.
keyTerminology.importance: More robust than z-score for skewed or heavy-tailed distributions; does not require assumptions of normality and is less sensitive to extreme outliers in the reference window.

keyTerminology.meaning: A robust measure of variability: MAD = median(|x_i - median(x)|). Used to form anomaly bounds as median +/- k*MAD, where k is typically 2.5-3. Equivalent to a robust z-score when scaled by 1.4826.
keyTerminology.importance: The most outlier-resistant of the univariate statistical detectors; does not break when a few historical observations are themselves anomalous, making it suitable for metrics with occasional spikes.

keyTerminology.meaning: A measure of distribution shift between a baseline and a current distribution: PSI = sum((A_i - E_i) * ln(A_i / E_i)) over bins, where A_i is the actual fraction and E_i is the expected fraction. PSI < 0.1 = stable, 0.1-0.2 = moderate shift, > 0.2 = significant shift.
keyTerminology.importance: The standard metric for detecting distribution drift in financial and ML-feature pipelines; quantifies not just whether a shift occurred but its magnitude across the full distribution, including tail behavior.

keyTerminology.meaning: A smoothing technique that computes a weighted average of historical values where recent observations receive exponentially more weight than older ones: EWMA_t = alpha * x_t + (1 - alpha) * EWMA_{t-1}.
keyTerminology.importance: Useful for gradual drift detection: when the current value diverges significantly from a slow-moving EWMA baseline, a subtle but persistent trend is flagged before it becomes a severe incident.

keyTerminology.meaning: The inability of a history-based anomaly detector to produce reliable bounds when insufficient historical data is available—typically during the first few weeks of monitoring a new table or metric.
keyTerminology.importance: Cold start is a common production failure mode: detectors either fire false positives from under-constrained models or must fall back to static thresholds until enough history accumulates, typically 2-4 weeks for daily metrics.

importantConcepts.concept: Static Thresholds vs Dynamic/Adaptive Anomaly Detection
importantConcepts.explanation: Static thresholds (e.g., 'alert if row count < 100,000') are simple to implement and audit but require an engineer to know in advance what values are abnormal and to update the threshold as data volumes grow or seasonal patterns shift. They catch only known failure modes—known-unknowns. Dynamic anomaly detection learns the normal distribution of a metric from history, automatically adapts to trends and seasonality, and flags deviations that no pre-written rule would have caught—unknown-unknowns. The production best practice is to combine both: hard static rules for absolute must-not-violate constraints (e.g., row count must never be zero) and dynamic detectors for drift, trend, and distributional anomalies. Dynamic detectors have higher false positive rates during cold start and require tuning of sensitivity parameters (window size, k-sigma, seasonality period), which static thresholds avoid.

Most data quality metrics exhibit strong seasonal patterns: order volumes are higher on weekdays than weekends, transaction counts spike at month-end, clickstream events peak in the evening. A naive anomaly detector trained on all recent history will have a high false-positive rate on low-volume weekend days (where the rolling mean overestimates normal volume) and will miss real drops on high-volume weekdays (where the rolling mean underestimates). Seasonality-aware detectors either compare the current observation only to same-day-of-week history (a simple but effective approach for daily metrics), or decompose the series into trend, seasonal, and residual components (STL decomposition), fitting the detector only to the residuals. More sophisticated tools like Prophet explicitly model multiple seasonalities (weekly, monthly, holiday effects) and generate a forecast with uncertainty bounds. Ignoring seasonality is the most common cause of alert fatigue in data quality monitoring.

importantConcepts.concept: Distribution Shift and PSI vs KS Test
importantConcepts.explanation: Volume anomalies (row count drops, null spikes) are the most visible failures, but many data quality incidents manifest as distribution shifts: the mean order amount creeps upward due to a price change, a feature used by an ML model changes its range after an upstream schema migration, or a traffic source changes the mix of user geographies. PSI and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test both detect distribution shift but with different strengths. PSI is a symmetric, interpretable, bin-based measure used widely in financial risk and ML monitoring; its output is a single scalar with conventional thresholds (0.1/0.2). The KS test is a non-parametric test that measures the maximum difference between two empirical CDFs and produces a p-value; it is more sensitive to differences in the center of the distribution and avoids arbitrary binning but is harder to interpret operationally. For ML feature monitoring, PSI is typically preferred because it quantifies impact magnitude; for hypothesis testing whether two samples come from the same distribution, KS is more principled.

For metrics with strong trends and seasonality, point-in-time statistical detectors (z-score on a rolling window) underperform because they conflate the trend component with the anomaly signal. Time-series decomposition separates a metric series into trend (long-term direction), seasonal (repeating pattern), and residual (noise + anomalies) components. STL (Seasonal and Trend decomposition using Loess) is a robust, computationally efficient decomposition that handles arbitrary seasonalities and is resilient to outliers. Prophet (Facebook/Meta, 2017) is a Bayesian additive model that fits trend + multiple seasonalities + holidays and generates a forecast with uncertainty intervals, making it directly usable as an anomaly detector by flagging actuals outside the predicted interval. ARIMA-style models (Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average) fit linear combinations of past values and errors; they handle autocorrelation well but require stationarity and are more complex to tune than STL or Prophet. For most data engineering anomaly detection use cases, STL residuals with a z-score on residuals or Prophet-generated bounds provide the best balance of accuracy and operational simplicity.

importantConcepts.concept: Alert Fatigue, Sensitivity Tuning, and False Positive vs False Negative Trade-off
importantConcepts.explanation: An anomaly detector with too-low a sensitivity threshold (e.g., k=1.5 sigma) will fire on routine variance, burying real incidents in noise and training teams to ignore alerts—alert fatigue. An over-conservative detector (k=5 sigma) misses genuine anomalies until they are severe. The optimal sensitivity depends on the metric's variance, business impact of missed incidents, and acceptable noise level. Practical tuning approaches include: backtesting the detector against a labeled historical incident log to measure precision and recall at different k values; setting different sensitivity levels for critical vs non-critical metrics; using a warm-up period before activating alerts on a new metric; and implementing alert deduplication (suppress a repeat alert for the same metric within N hours). Rolling window length also matters—shorter windows (7 days) react faster but are noisier; longer windows (90 days) are stable but slow to adapt to legitimate step-changes in data volumes. Most production systems land on 28-day same-day-of-week windows with k=3 as a starting point, then tune per metric.

variationsAndTypes: **Point anomaly detection:** A single observation is far from the expected range (e.g., today's row count is 3 standard deviations below the rolling mean).

**Contextual anomaly detection:** An observation is anomalous in its context but not globally (e.g., 10,000 rows on a Sunday is normal but would be anomalous on a Monday given the known weekly pattern).

**Collective anomaly detection:** A sequence of observations is collectively anomalous even if no single point is extreme (e.g., a week-long gradual row-count decline that STL decomposition or EWMA catches as drift).
**Volume/freshness anomaly detection:** Monitoring row counts, record counts, and ingestion timestamps for drops, spikes, or delays—the most common and highest-signal anomaly type for data pipelines.
**Null/completeness anomaly detection:** Tracking null rates per column over time and flagging sudden spikes (upstream schema change, JOIN nullification, ETL bug) that exceed historical norms.

**Distribution anomaly detection (data drift):** Comparing statistical distributions (PSI, KS) between historical baseline and current batch, essential for ML feature monitoring and catching subtle upstream data changes.
**Schema/metadata anomaly detection:** Detecting unexpected column additions, removals, type changes, or cardinality explosions that indicate upstream schema drift.
advantages: **Catches unknown-unknowns:** Detects data quality incidents that no human would have anticipated or written a static rule for, including novel upstream bugs, infrastructure changes, and business-pattern shifts.
**Adapts automatically:** Dynamic baselines adjust to trends, seasonality, and legitimate growth in data volumes without requiring manual threshold updates.
**Scales to hundreds of metrics:** A single parameterized detector can monitor any numeric metric time series, making it feasible to monitor all tables and columns in a large warehouse.

**Reduces mean-time-to-detection:** Automated detection that runs at every pipeline completion catches incidents within hours rather than the days it takes for stakeholders to notice corrupt dashboards.
disadvantages: **Cold-start problem:** Requires 2-6 weeks of historical data before producing reliable bounds; new tables or metrics need static fallback thresholds during warm-up.
**Alert fatigue risk:** Poorly tuned sensitivity or failure to handle seasonality produces high false-positive rates that desensitize on-call engineers to real incidents.

**Explainability challenge:** Statistical and ML-based anomaly scores are harder to explain to business stakeholders than a simple static rule (e.g., 'row count was 6 standard deviations below the 28-day Tuesday average').

**Does not catch logical errors:** Anomaly detection identifies statistical deviations but cannot detect that values are systematically wrong but consistent (e.g., prices denominated in the wrong currency but always within the expected range).

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use dynamic anomaly detection on high-value, widely consumed tables with at least 2-4 weeks of stable history, where the cost of a missed incident exceeds the cost of occasional false positives and where static thresholds would require constant manual updates due to seasonality or growth. Combine with static rules for hard absolute constraints.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid dynamic anomaly detection during cold-start periods without a static fallback, for highly irregular one-off or exploratory datasets without stable historical patterns, or when the business requires explicit, auditable threshold rules rather than statistical model outputs (e.g., regulated reporting with deterministic pass/fail criteria).

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Anomaly detection on data quality metrics is like a bank's fraud detection system applied to your own pipeline's health. The bank does not write a rule for every possible fraudulent transaction pattern; instead it learns what your spending behavior looks like over time—where you shop, how much, at what time of day—and flags transactions that deviate significantly from that learned profile. Similarly, a data quality anomaly detector learns that your orders table always loads between 130,000 and 160,000 rows on Tuesdays and that the null rate on order_id has never exceeded 0.5%. When today's Tuesday load brings 42,000 rows and a 3% null rate, it fires an alert—even though no one wrote a rule for those specific values—because they are statistically implausible given everything it knows about your pipeline's history.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A static threshold (e.g., alert if row count < 100,000) is sufficient for data quality monitoring.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Static thresholds only catch failure modes you anticipated when writing the rule and break silently when data volumes grow or seasonal patterns shift. They generate false positives on low-volume weekends and miss gradual drops on weekdays. Dynamic anomaly detection is needed to catch the far larger category of unknown-unknown failures.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A low z-score threshold means better anomaly detection.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Lowering the z-score threshold (e.g., from 3 to 1.5) increases sensitivity but dramatically increases false positive rates, causing alert fatigue. The right threshold depends on the metric's inherent variance, seasonal patterns, and the cost of missed vs false incidents. Tuning requires backtesting against historical incidents, not just setting a low number.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Distribution shift detection is only relevant for ML pipelines.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Distribution shifts in operational data metrics—order amounts, user ages, event latencies—indicate upstream process changes that corrupt downstream analytics even when row counts and null rates look normal. PSI and KS tests are equally valuable in non-ML data quality pipelines for catching subtle upstream schema or business-logic changes.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Store metrics history in a partitioned table (by table_name, metric_name, date) and run detectors via SQL window functions pushed down to the warehouse; avoid pulling history into Python for large metric sets. Materialize rolling statistics (mean, std, percentiles) incrementally so each run only reads the latest window, not full history.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Make metric computation idempotent (use INSERT OR REPLACE / MERGE patterns keyed on table_name + metric_name + partition_date) so pipeline reruns do not duplicate history entries. Ensure anomaly detector failures do not block pipeline promotion—degrade gracefully to static thresholds or log-and-continue if the detector errors.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Separate the metric computation step from the anomaly detection step so a detector failure does not prevent metrics from being recorded for future use. Back up the metrics history store and treat it as a first-class data asset with the same durability guarantees as production tables.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Monitor the monitors: track alert volume, false positive rate (based on engineer acknowledgements), and detection latency over time. Alert on gaps in metric history (missing runs indicate metric computation failures). Dashboard the health of the anomaly detection system itself alongside the pipelines it monitors.
productionConsiderations.security: Metrics history may expose sensitive statistical summaries (mean order amount, user count by segment) even without raw data; apply appropriate access controls. Avoid including sample failing values in alert messages unless they are confirmed non-PII.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Compute cheap metrics (row count, null count, max timestamp) at every pipeline run; compute expensive metrics (full-column distribution histograms, PSI) on a daily or weekly cadence. Use approximate algorithms (T-Digest, HyperLogLog) for percentile and distinct-count metrics at scale to avoid full-sort operations.
productionConsiderations.performance: Use SQL window functions (AVG, STDDEV_POP, PERCENTILE_CONT) over the metrics history table rather than pulling data into Python; execute detection queries on the warehouse where the data lives. For distribution-shift detection, pre-bin histograms at write time to avoid recomputing bins at detection time.

codeExamples.title: Seasonality-Aware Z-Score / MAD Anomaly Detector (Python)
codeExamples.overview: A Python function that takes a pandas Series of daily metric values (e.g., row counts indexed by date) and detects anomalies using both z-score and MAD methods with a same-day-of-week rolling window to handle weekly seasonality. Returns flagged anomaly dates and computed bounds.
codeExamples.code:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from typing import Tuple

def detect_anomalies_rolling(
    series: pd.Series,
    k_zscore: float = 3.0,
    k_mad: float = 3.0,
    min_history: int = 8,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """
    Seasonality-aware anomaly detector using z-score and MAD on a rolling
    same-day-of-week window.

    Parameters
    ----------
    series      : pd.Series with DatetimeIndex and numeric metric values
    k_zscore    : z-score threshold (default 3.0 sigma)
    k_mad       : MAD threshold multiplier (default 3.0)
    min_history : minimum same-DOW observations required before scoring

    Returns
    -------
    pd.DataFrame with columns: date, value, dow_mean, dow_std, dow_median,
    dow_mad, z_score, mad_score, lower_zscore, upper_zscore,
    lower_mad, upper_mad, is_anomaly_zscore, is_anomaly_mad, is_anomaly
    """
    if not isinstance(series.index, pd.DatetimeIndex):
        raise ValueError("series must have a DatetimeIndex")

    series = series.sort_index()
    results = []

    for i, (date, value) in enumerate(series.items()):
        dow = date.dayofweek  # 0=Monday, 6=Sunday

        # Select same-day-of-week history BEFORE current date
        history = series[
            (series.index < date) & (series.index.dayofweek == dow)
        ]

        if len(history) < min_history:
            # Cold start: insufficient history, skip scoring
            results.append({
                "date": date, "value": value,
                "dow_mean": np.nan, "dow_std": np.nan,
                "dow_median": np.nan, "dow_mad": np.nan,
                "z_score": np.nan, "mad_score": np.nan,
                "lower_zscore": np.nan, "upper_zscore": np.nan,
                "lower_mad": np.nan, "upper_mad": np.nan,
                "is_anomaly_zscore": False,
                "is_anomaly_mad": False,
                "is_anomaly": False,
            })
            continue

        dow_mean = history.mean()
        dow_std = history.std(ddof=1)
        dow_median = history.median()
        # MAD scaled to be consistent with std under normality
        dow_mad = (history - dow_median).abs().median() * 1.4826

        z = (value - dow_mean) / dow_std if dow_std > 0 else 0.0
        mad_z = (value - dow_median) / dow_mad if dow_mad > 0 else 0.0

        results.append({
            "date": date,
            "value": value,
            "dow_mean": round(dow_mean, 2),
            "dow_std": round(dow_std, 2),
            "dow_median": round(dow_median, 2),
            "dow_mad": round(dow_mad, 2),
            "z_score": round(z, 3),
            "mad_score": round(mad_z, 3),
            "lower_zscore": round(dow_mean - k_zscore * dow_std, 2),
            "upper_zscore": round(dow_mean + k_zscore * dow_std, 2),
            "lower_mad": round(dow_median - k_mad * dow_mad, 2),
            "upper_mad": round(dow_median + k_mad * dow_mad, 2),
            "is_anomaly_zscore": abs(z) > k_zscore,
            "is_anomaly_mad": abs(mad_z) > k_mad,
            "is_anomaly": abs(z) > k_zscore or abs(mad_z) > k_mad,
        })

    df = pd.DataFrame(results)
    anomalies = df[df["is_anomaly"]]
    print(f"Checked {len(df)} observations | Anomalies: {len(anomalies)}")
    if not anomalies.empty:
        for _, row in anomalies.iterrows():
            print(
                f"  ANOMALY {row['date'].date()} value={row['value']:,.0f} "
                f"z={row['z_score']:.2f} "
                f"bounds_zscore=[{row['lower_zscore']:,.0f}, {row['upper_zscore']:,.0f}]"
            )
    return df


# --- Example usage ---
np.random.seed(42)
dates = pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=90, freq="D")
# Simulate row counts: ~100k base, weekend dip ~40%, some noise
base = np.where(dates.dayofweek < 5, 100_000, 60_000).astype(float)
noise = np.random.normal(0, 3_000, size=90)
row_counts = pd.Series(base + noise, index=dates)

# Inject two anomalies
row_counts.iloc[75] = 32_000   # severe Tuesday drop (anomaly)
row_counts.iloc[82] = 145_000  # spike on a Wednesday (anomaly)

result_df = detect_anomalies_rolling(row_counts, k_zscore=3.0, k_mad=3.0)
codeExamples.breakdown: The function filters history to only same-day-of-week observations before the current date, providing seasonality-aware baselines. The z-score uses mean and sample standard deviation; the MAD score uses median and scaled MAD (multiplied by 1.4826 to match the standard deviation under normality). The cold-start guard (`min_history=8`) skips scoring until at least 8 same-DOW observations exist. Both methods flag independently; `is_anomaly` is the union so either detector triggers an alert. The final print loop surfaces anomaly dates with their observed values and bounds for immediate debugging.

codeExamples.commonIssues: Not sorting the series by date before slicing, causing future data to leak into the history window. Setting k too low (e.g., 1.5) on high-variance metrics, causing alert fatigue. Forgetting the 1.4826 scaling factor for MAD, making it incomparable to the z-score scale. Using ddof=0 (population std) on small windows, which underestimates variance.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: For large-scale use (thousands of metrics), push the rolling window statistics computation into SQL using STDDEV_POP and AVG window functions over the metrics_history table rather than running this per-metric in Python. Cache the historical statistics per metric per day-of-week in a precomputed table updated incrementally, so the detector queries a single row rather than recomputing from full history each run.

codeExamples.title: Distribution Shift Detection: PSI and KS Test (Python)
codeExamples.overview: Compute Population Stability Index (PSI) and run a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test between a baseline distribution and a current distribution of a numeric column. Interpret results with actionable thresholds. Applicable to both data quality monitoring and ML feature drift detection.
codeExamples.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from typing import Optional


def compute_psi(
    baseline: np.ndarray,
    current: np.ndarray,
    n_bins: int = 10,
    epsilon: float = 1e-6,
) -> dict:
    """
    Compute Population Stability Index (PSI) between baseline and current.

    PSI < 0.1  : no significant shift (stable)
    PSI 0.1-0.2: moderate shift (investigate)
    PSI > 0.2  : significant shift (alert)

    Parameters
    ----------
    baseline : 1-D array of reference distribution values
    current  : 1-D array of current distribution values
    n_bins   : number of equal-width bins (default 10)
    epsilon  : small constant to avoid log(0)
    """
    # Derive bin edges from combined range
    combined_min = min(baseline.min(), current.min())
    combined_max = max(baseline.max(), current.max())
    bins = np.linspace(combined_min, combined_max, n_bins + 1)

    # Compute normalized bin frequencies
    base_counts, _ = np.histogram(baseline, bins=bins)
    curr_counts, _ = np.histogram(current, bins=bins)

    base_pct = base_counts / len(baseline) + epsilon
    curr_pct = curr_counts / len(current) + epsilon

    # PSI formula: sum( (actual - expected) * ln(actual / expected) )
    psi_per_bin = (curr_pct - base_pct) * np.log(curr_pct / base_pct)
    psi = psi_per_bin.sum()

    return {
        "psi": round(float(psi), 5),
        "interpretation": (
            "stable" if psi < 0.1
            else "moderate shift" if psi < 0.2
            else "SIGNIFICANT SHIFT"
        ),
        "bins": bins.tolist(),
        "baseline_pct": base_pct.tolist(),
        "current_pct": curr_pct.tolist(),
        "psi_per_bin": psi_per_bin.tolist(),
    }


def compute_ks_test(
    baseline: np.ndarray,
    current: np.ndarray,
    alpha: float = 0.05,
) -> dict:
    """
    Two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test between baseline and current.
    Returns statistic, p-value, and whether to reject H0 (same distribution).
    """
    ks_stat, p_value = stats.ks_2samp(baseline, current)
    return {
        "ks_statistic": round(float(ks_stat), 5),
        "p_value": round(float(p_value), 6),
        "reject_h0": bool(p_value < alpha),
        "interpretation": (
            f"DISTRIBUTION SHIFT DETECTED (p={p_value:.4f} < {alpha})"
            if p_value < alpha
            else f"No significant shift (p={p_value:.4f} >= {alpha})"
        ),
    }


def check_distribution_shift(
    baseline: np.ndarray,
    current: np.ndarray,
    column_name: str = "feature",
    psi_threshold: float = 0.2,
    ks_alpha: float = 0.05,
) -> bool:
    """Run PSI and KS test; print results; return True if shift detected."""
    print(f"\n=== Distribution Shift Check: {column_name} ===")
    print(f"  Baseline: n={len(baseline)}, mean={baseline.mean():.2f}, "
          f"std={baseline.std():.2f}, p50={np.median(baseline):.2f}")
    print(f"  Current:  n={len(current)},  mean={current.mean():.2f}, "
          f"std={current.std():.2f}, p50={np.median(current):.2f}")

    psi_result = compute_psi(baseline, current)
    ks_result = compute_ks_test(baseline, current, alpha=ks_alpha)

    print(f"  PSI = {psi_result['psi']} -> {psi_result['interpretation']}")
    print(f"  KS  = {ks_result['interpretation']}")

    shift_detected = (
        psi_result["psi"] >= psi_threshold or ks_result["reject_h0"]
    )
    print(f"  Shift Detected: {shift_detected}")
    return shift_detected


# --- Example: order_amount column, baseline vs current month ---
np.random.seed(0)
# Baseline: lognormal order amounts, mean ~$85, std ~$30
baseline_amounts = np.random.lognormal(mean=4.45, sigma=0.35, size=5000)
# Current: shifted distribution, mean ~$120 (price increase)
current_amounts = np.random.lognormal(mean=4.79, sigma=0.40, size=5000)

alert = check_distribution_shift(
    baseline_amounts, current_amounts,
    column_name="order_amount",
    psi_threshold=0.2,
    ks_alpha=0.05,
)

if alert:
    print("\nACTION: Investigate upstream price change or currency conversion bug.")
codeExamples.breakdown: The PSI function bins both distributions on the same edges (derived from the combined range to ensure fair comparison), adds a small epsilon to avoid log(0) for empty bins, and applies the standard PSI formula. The result dictionary includes per-bin contributions so the caller can identify which value ranges are driving the shift. The KS test uses scipy's `ks_2samp`, which compares empirical CDFs directly without binning, producing a p-value under the null hypothesis that both samples come from the same distribution. `check_distribution_shift` runs both, prints summary statistics for quick comparison, and returns a boolean alert flag for pipeline integration.

  Current:  n=5000,  mean=121.87, std=49.03, p50=115.44

  KS  = DISTRIBUTION SHIFT DETECTED (p=0.0000 < 0.05)

codeExamples.commonIssues: Using different bin edges for baseline and current when computing PSI, making bins incomparable and producing an inflated PSI. Applying PSI to categorical or boolean columns without appropriate handling. Not checking sample sizes: KS test loses power with very small samples (n < 30) and is overly sensitive with very large samples (n > 100,000), requiring effect-size interpretation alongside the p-value.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: For large tables, compute histogram bins in SQL (using WIDTH_BUCKET or NTILE) rather than pulling all values into Python. Pre-compute and store baseline histograms once per baseline period, then at detection time only compute current histograms and apply the PSI formula—this reduces per-run cost from O(n_rows) to O(n_bins). Use T-Digest approximate percentiles for memory-efficient distribution summaries at scale.

codeExamples.title: SQL Rolling Anomaly Detection on Metrics History Table
codeExamples.overview: A SQL query that reads from a metrics_history table, computes a rolling mean and standard deviation over the last N same-day-of-week observations using window functions, and flags today's metric as anomalous if it falls outside mean +/- 3*stddev. Designed to run directly in the warehouse as part of a post-load quality check.
codeExamples.code:
-- Anomaly detection on metrics_history table using SQL window functions.
-- Assumes a table: metrics_history(table_name, metric_name, partition_date, value)
-- Run after each pipeline load to flag anomalies without pulling data into Python.

WITH
-- Step 1: Annotate each row with its day-of-week for seasonality grouping
metrics_with_dow AS (
    SELECT
        table_name,
        metric_name,
        partition_date,
        value,
        EXTRACT(DOW FROM partition_date)  AS day_of_week,  -- 0=Sun, 6=Sat in most SQL dialects
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY table_name, metric_name, EXTRACT(DOW FROM partition_date)
            ORDER BY partition_date DESC
        ) AS dow_recency_rank  -- 1 = most recent same-DOW observation
    FROM metrics_history
    WHERE partition_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '120 days'  -- limit scan window
),

-- Step 2: Compute rolling stats over the last 28 same-DOW observations (excluding today)
dow_stats AS (
    SELECT
        table_name,
        metric_name,
        day_of_week,
        AVG(value)                                AS dow_mean,
        STDDEV_POP(value)                         AS dow_stddev,
        PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP
            (ORDER BY value)                      AS dow_median,
        COUNT(*)                                  AS history_count
    FROM metrics_with_dow
    WHERE dow_recency_rank BETWEEN 2 AND 29  -- rows 2-29 = last 28, skipping rank 1 (today)
    GROUP BY table_name, metric_name, day_of_week
),

-- Step 3: Join today's values to their DOW stats
today_metrics AS (
    SELECT *
    FROM metrics_with_dow
    WHERE dow_recency_rank = 1  -- most recent observation = today
      AND partition_date = CURRENT_DATE
)

-- Step 4: Compute z-score and flag anomalies
SELECT
    t.table_name,
    t.metric_name,
    t.partition_date,
    t.value                                                    AS current_value,
    s.dow_mean,
    s.dow_stddev,
    s.history_count,
    s.dow_mean - 3 * s.dow_stddev                             AS lower_bound,
    s.dow_mean + 3 * s.dow_stddev                             AS upper_bound,
    CASE
        WHEN s.dow_stddev = 0 THEN 0
        ELSE (t.value - s.dow_mean) / s.dow_stddev
    END                                                        AS z_score,
    CASE
        WHEN s.history_count < 8
            THEN 'INSUFFICIENT_HISTORY'
        WHEN s.dow_stddev = 0
            THEN 'ZERO_VARIANCE'
        WHEN t.value < s.dow_mean - 3 * s.dow_stddev
            THEN 'ANOMALY_LOW'
        WHEN t.value > s.dow_mean + 3 * s.dow_stddev
            THEN 'ANOMALY_HIGH'
        ELSE 'OK'
    END                                                        AS anomaly_status
FROM today_metrics t
LEFT JOIN dow_stats s
    ON  t.table_name  = s.table_name
    AND t.metric_name = s.metric_name
    AND t.day_of_week = s.day_of_week
ORDER BY
    CASE WHEN anomaly_status IN ('ANOMALY_LOW', 'ANOMALY_HIGH') THEN 0 ELSE 1 END,
    ABS(z_score) DESC NULLS LAST;
codeExamples.breakdown: The CTE `metrics_with_dow` uses `ROW_NUMBER()` partitioned by table, metric, and day-of-week to rank observations chronologically within each day-of-week bucket. `dow_stats` filters to ranks 2-29, which are the 28 most recent same-DOW historical observations excluding today, and computes `AVG`, `STDDEV_POP`, and the median via `PERCENTILE_CONT`. `today_metrics` selects rank-1 (today) entries. The final select joins today's values to their historical statistics, computes the z-score, and derives the `anomaly_status` flag, including `INSUFFICIENT_HISTORY` for cold-start safety. The ORDER BY surfaces anomalies at the top, ranked by absolute z-score severity.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Using STDDEV_SAMP instead of STDDEV_POP on small windows produces inflated standard deviations that make the bounds too wide. EXTRACT(DOW) behavior differs between SQL dialects (Snowflake, BigQuery, PostgreSQL, Redshift): verify that 0=Sunday or 0=Monday consistently for your platform. Not filtering the history scan window (the `INTERVAL '120 days'` filter) can cause the CTE to scan years of history and explode query cost.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Materialize the DOW statistics as a separate incremental table updated nightly, so the detection query joins precomputed stats rather than recomputing from raw history on every run. Cluster or partition the metrics_history table by (table_name, metric_name) so the window function scan is narrow. On Snowflake, use `QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1` to avoid the CTE fan-out and run the filter inline.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A fintech company processes millions of payment transactions daily and serves a real-time fraud model and executive revenue dashboards. Twice in the past quarter, silent pipeline failures—a 35% row-count drop due to a Kafka consumer lag and a null spike in merchant_id due to an upstream schema migration—went undetected for 18 and 11 hours respectively, corrupting revenue metrics and causing the fraud model to make predictions on incomplete feature data. The team needs automated anomaly detection on pipeline metrics so incidents are caught within one pipeline cycle (30 minutes) rather than after stakeholders report wrong numbers.
endToEndExample.inputData: A metrics_history table populated after each pipeline run with: table_name (e.g., 'transactions', 'merchant_features'), metric_name ('row_count', 'null_rate_merchant_id', 'distinct_user_count', 'mean_amount', 'p95_amount', 'freshness_lag_minutes'), partition_date, value, and computed_at timestamp. History spans 90 days across 12 monitored tables and 6 metrics each = 72 metric time series.
endToEndExample.architecture: Airflow DAG: (1) Transaction load job -> (2) Metric computation step (SQL, appends to metrics_history) -> (3) Anomaly detection step (SQL window function query) -> (4) Distribution shift step (Python, PSI on amount distribution) -> (5) Alert routing (PagerDuty for P1, Slack for P2) -> (6) Dashboard refresh. Metrics history stored in Snowflake. Monte Carlo monitors freshness and schema changes in parallel as a secondary layer.
processingSteps: 1. The transaction load job completes and a post-load SQL step computes 6 metrics for the transactions table: row_count, null_rate_merchant_id, distinct_user_count, mean_amount, p95_amount, and freshness_lag_minutes, inserting one row per metric into metrics_history.

2. The SQL rolling anomaly detection query runs against metrics_history, comparing each metric's current value to the mean and stddev of the last 28 same-day-of-week observations with STDDEV_POP and a 3-sigma bound. Today's row_count=1,820,000 versus DOW_mean=2,650,000 produces z=-14.2, flagged as ANOMALY_LOW.

3. The Python PSI step pulls today's and last month's amount histogram bins from pre-computed Snowflake histogram tables, computes PSI=0.09 (stable), and the KS test p-value=0.41 (no shift). The distribution is clean; the problem is volume, not composition.

4. The alert routing step classifies z-score < -10 as P1 (revenue-impacting), fires a PagerDuty alert to the on-call data engineer with: table=transactions, metric=row_count, current=1,820,000, expected_range=[2,380,000, 2,920,000], z_score=-14.2, last_good_run=yesterday 02:15 UTC.

5. The on-call engineer investigates and finds Kafka consumer group lag spiked to 4.2 hours due to a broker rebalance, causing the pipeline to process only 68% of today's transactions. The Kafka team is paged and the consumer group is reset.

6. After the reprocessing completes, the pipeline re-runs from the load step. The anomaly detection step clears (row_count=2,680,000, z=+0.14, status=OK) and a resolution Slack message confirms the incident is closed.
endToEndExample.output: Zero data quality incidents reaching downstream consumers; the fraud model receives a complete feature table; the revenue dashboard reflects accurate same-day transaction volumes. Incident metrics: time-to-detection=18 minutes (one pipeline cycle after the anomaly), time-to-resolution=2.5 hours (vs 18 hours in the previous manual-detection incident).
endToEndExample.monitoring: A Grafana dashboard shows real-time anomaly status (OK / ANOMALY_LOW / ANOMALY_HIGH / INSUFFICIENT_HISTORY) for all 72 metric time series, a 30-day rolling view of each metric with bounds overlaid, alert volume and false positive rate per week, and mean-time-to-detection trended over the last quarter. Monte Carlo surfaces freshness lag and schema change alerts in a separate feed.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: If the metric computation step fails (e.g., the SQL query times out), it logs the error, does not insert into metrics_history, and sends a monitoring alert that the health metrics are stale. The anomaly detection step checks for missing today's entries and produces a 'MISSING_METRIC' status rather than a false negative, routing a separate alert that metric computation itself failed. Anomaly alerts include a lineage link to all downstream consumers (dashboards, ML models, reports) so the impact can be assessed immediately.
endToEndExample.finalResult: The fintech's data platform detects anomalies in pipeline metrics within one pipeline cycle (30 minutes) rather than after stakeholder complaints. The fraud model's feature freshness SLA (data available within 60 minutes of run completion) is now operationally enforced. Over the first quarter of deployment, the system fired 94 alerts: 87 true positives (root causes: Kafka lag, upstream schema migrations, a misconfigured ETL duplicate load, and two upstream source delays), 7 false positives (all from a seasonal holiday week not yet in the 90-day history window, resolved by adding the holiday flag to the DOW grouping).

industryUseCases.problem: Transaction volume and feature distributions for fraud and risk models needed continuous monitoring across time zones, payment methods, and merchant categories. Manual threshold rules required constant updates as the business grew and seasonal patterns shifted, and distribution shifts in merchant_category or transaction_amount distributions could silently degrade model performance before the next scheduled retraining.
industryUseCases.solution: Stripe built an internal data observability system that tracks hundreds of pipeline metrics with adaptive, seasonality-aware anomaly detection, using time-series decomposition to separate business trends from true anomalies. industryUseCases.problem: Data teams at large enterprises needed anomaly detection that could spin up on new tables with minimal configuration, handle the cold-start problem gracefully, and reduce alert fatigue enough that engineers actually trusted and acted on alerts rather than ignoring them.

Column-level distribution monitoring and correlation analysis between metrics enable root-cause hypothesis generation alongside the anomaly flag.

The platform's automated sensitivity calibration makes it practical to monitor all columns on all production tables rather than a manually selected subset, expanding coverage without expanding on-call workload.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Push metric computation and rolling statistic computation into the warehouse using SQL window functions over a partitioned metrics_history table; avoid pulling large time series into Python for large-scale deployments (hundreds of tables, thousands of metrics). Use approximate algorithms (T-Digest for percentiles, HyperLogLog for distinct counts) where exact computation would require full-table sorts. Partition the metrics_history table by (table_name, metric_name, partition_date) and cluster by partition_date so window function scans are narrow and cheap. For distribution-shift detection at scale, pre-compute histogram bins at write time rather than recomputing the raw distributions at detection time.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Separate the metric computation step from the anomaly detection step in the orchestration DAG so a detection failure (e.g., insufficient history, SQL timeout) does not prevent metric collection, which is needed for future detection runs. Make metric insertion idempotent using MERGE or INSERT OR REPLACE on (table_name, metric_name, partition_date) as the natural key, so pipeline reruns do not duplicate history. Implement a 'MISSING_METRIC' status for cases where today's metric was not recorded, so the detector raises an alert about its own data gap rather than silently producing a false negative.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Store the metrics_history table on a durable, replicated warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift) rather than a single-node database. Route anomaly detection alerts through a reliable message bus (PagerDuty, OpsGenie) with acknowledgement tracking so alert delivery is guaranteed and alert state is visible to all on-call team members. Run the anomaly detection job as a separate DAG from the main pipeline DAG with independent retry logic so a main pipeline failure does not also silence the anomaly detector.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Back up the metrics_history table with point-in-time recovery capability; it is the institutional memory of pipeline health and losing it means losing all baselines and cold-starting all detectors. Document the current detector configuration (window size, k-sigma thresholds, seasonality groupings) in version control alongside pipeline code so the detection setup can be recreated after a disaster. After a pipeline outage and reprocessing, back-fill metric history for the affected days before re-enabling detectors to avoid spurious anomalies from the gap in history.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Materialize daily DOW statistics (mean, stddev, count) per metric as a precomputed table updated incrementally at the end of each day, so the detection query is a simple join rather than a recomputation from raw history. For Python-based distribution shift detection, store pre-binned histograms (as JSON arrays) in the metrics_history table rather than raw sample values, so PSI computation at detection time reads O(n_bins) rows rather than O(n_rows). Cache detector outputs in a results table so the alert routing step can be a simple SELECT on the latest anomaly statuses rather than rerunning detection.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Compute cheap metrics (row count, null count, max timestamp) after every pipeline run; compute expensive metrics (full-column distribution histograms, cross-column correlation, PSI) on a daily or weekly cadence. Use approximate distinct counts (HyperLogLog) instead of COUNT(DISTINCT) for high-cardinality columns on large tables, reducing both compute and scan cost. Tier monitoring rigor by table importance: critical production tables (revenue, fraud features) get full metric coverage with low k-sigma thresholds; intermediate staging tables get lightweight row-count and freshness checks only.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Metrics history may contain statistical summaries that reveal sensitive business information (e.g., daily transaction volumes, mean order amounts by segment) even without raw data; apply column-level security or row-level access control to metrics_history so only authorized roles can query all tables' metrics. Avoid including sample failing values (which may contain PII) in anomaly alert messages; reference the failing metric and its value, not the underlying data rows. Treat the anomaly detection system's configuration (threshold settings, monitored columns) as sensitive operational data and store it with appropriate access controls.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Monitor the anomaly detection system itself: track the fraction of metrics in INSUFFICIENT_HISTORY (indicates cold-start or metric computation failures), the weekly alert count and engineer-acknowledged false positive rate, and the end-to-end detection latency (time from pipeline completion to alert delivery). Dashboard all 72 metric time series with rolling bounds overlaid so the team can visually validate detector behavior. Set up a separate alert on metric computation staleness (e.g., if no metric row was inserted for a table in the last 25 hours, alert that the health monitoring is blind).
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Validate the metrics_history table itself: check that each monitored (table_name, metric_name) pair has a row for every expected partition_date (no gaps), that values are within physically plausible ranges (row counts are non-negative, null rates are 0-1), and that the computed_at timestamp is within a reasonable window of partition_date. Apply the same anomaly detection principles recursively: if the metrics history itself has anomalies (unexpected gaps, value spikes), that is a signal of metric computation failures rather than true pipeline anomalies.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log each anomaly detection run with: run_timestamp, metrics evaluated, anomalies detected (count), anomalies suppressed (deduplication), and alerts sent. For each alert, log: table_name, metric_name, current_value, dow_mean, lower_bound, upper_bound, z_score, anomaly_status, alert_channel, and delivery_status. Implement alert suppression: if the same (table, metric) anomaly fired in the last N hours and has not been resolved, suppress repeat alerts to avoid flooding the on-call channel. Route P1 anomalies (|z| > 10 or business-critical tables) to PagerDuty with escalation; route P2 anomalies to Slack with table owner tagged for async triage.

recommendedPractices: **Start with volume and freshness metrics** (row count, null rate, max timestamp) before adding distribution-level monitoring; they are cheapest to compute, highest signal, and require no special handling for cold-start.

**Use same-day-of-week baselines** for daily metrics rather than naive rolling windows; this is the single most effective change to reduce false positives from weekly seasonality without needing a full time-series model.

**Combine static and dynamic thresholds:** use hard static rules for absolute must-not-violate constraints (row count > 0, null rate < 10%) alongside z-score/MAD-based dynamic detection for deviation from historical norms.

**Implement a warm-up period:** disable dynamic anomaly alerts (but continue recording metrics) for the first 14-28 days on a new table or metric until sufficient same-DOW history exists; fall back to static thresholds during warm-up.

**Tune sensitivity per metric:** critical revenue or ML-feature metrics warrant tighter k-sigma (2.5) and lower alert thresholds; high-variance exploratory metrics should use wider bounds (3.5+) or be omitted from paging alerts.
engineeringStandards: Anomaly detection configuration (window size, k-sigma, monitored metrics, alert routing) lives in version control alongside pipeline code and is reviewed as part of pipeline PRs.
Every monitored metric must have a defined owner (team and individual) who receives and is responsible for triaging its alerts.
Anomaly detection results are stored in a results table (not just sent as alerts) so incident post-mortems can query historical anomaly flags alongside raw pipeline metrics.
designRecommendations: Separate metric computation from anomaly detection in the DAG: metric computation is critical-path (must succeed for data quality monitoring), detection is advisory (failure should alert but not block pipeline promotion).

Design the metrics_history schema with (table_name, metric_name, partition_date) as a composite key and add a metadata column for metric_type (volume / null_rate / distribution) so detection queries can filter efficiently.

For distribution-shift detection, pre-bin histograms at metric computation time using fixed bin edges derived from the baseline period, and store bin frequencies as a JSON array in metrics_history to keep distribution state without raw data.
namingConventions: Name anomaly alert severity levels consistently: P1 (revenue/ML-impacting, page on-call), P2 (data quality degradation, Slack alert), P3 (informational, dashboard only).
Name history and results tables consistently: `dq_metrics_history`, `dq_anomaly_results`, `dq_distribution_histograms`.
documentationStandards: Document each monitored metric: what it measures, why it matters, the detection method used (z-score/MAD/PSI), the sensitivity setting (k-sigma/PSI threshold), and who owns the alert.
Maintain a runbook per monitored table covering: common anomaly patterns, how to investigate each alert type, known seasonal patterns (e.g., month-end spikes, holiday dips), and the escalation path.
Record false positive incidents in a shared log with root cause (e.g., 'holiday week not in 90-day history') so the team can improve the detector configuration over time.
testingStrategies: Backtest detectors against a labeled historical incident log (anomalies confirmed by post-mortems) before deploying to production, measuring precision and recall at different k-sigma values.

Inject synthetic anomalies into a staging metrics_history table (row count drops of -20%, -50%, -80%; null rate spikes from 0.1% to 5%, 20%) and verify that detectors fire at the expected severity thresholds.
Test cold-start behavior by running the detector against a table with only 3 days of history and confirming it returns INSUFFICIENT_HISTORY rather than false positive alerts.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a naive rolling window (all recent N days) without day-of-week grouping for daily metrics.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Engineers implement z-score over the last 28 calendar days without considering that weekend volumes are structurally lower than weekday volumes, blending the two into a single baseline.
commonMistakes.impact: False positive alerts every weekend (low weekend values look anomalous against a weekday-dominated mean) and missed real anomalies on high-volume weekdays (a 20% drop still looks within the wide variance band). Alert fatigue causes the team to stop acting on alerts.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Group history by day-of-week (EXTRACT(DOW)) and compute mean/stddev only over same-DOW observations. For metrics with multiple seasonalities (weekly + monthly), use STL decomposition or Prophet to fully account for cyclical patterns.

commonMistakes.mistake: Deploying dynamic anomaly detection without a cold-start fallback on new tables.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Engineers copy a working anomaly detection DAG to a new table and activate alerts immediately, before the detector has accumulated sufficient same-DOW history.
commonMistakes.impact: The detector fires with extremely wide or nonsensical bounds during the first 2-3 weeks, generating false positive alerts on every run. The team disables the detector or ignores it, losing coverage exactly when a new table is most likely to have teething quality issues.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Implement a minimum history guard (e.g., `history_count < 8 -> INSUFFICIENT_HISTORY`) that suppresses anomaly alerts and falls back to static threshold rules during warm-up. Log metrics from day one, but only enable dynamic anomaly alerting after 14-28 days of clean history.

commonMistakes.mistake: Monitoring only row counts and missing distribution-level anomalies.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Row count is the easiest metric to compute and monitor, and teams stop there assuming volume checks are sufficient for data quality assurance.
commonMistakes.impact: Distribution shifts—a sudden change in the mean transaction amount due to a currency conversion bug, a change in the range of a feature used by an ML model, a shift in the mix of event types—are completely invisible to volume-only monitors. These incidents quietly corrupt analytics and degrade model performance without triggering any alert.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Extend monitoring to include null rates per critical column, mean and p95 of key numeric columns, and PSI/KS distribution checks between the current batch and a 30-day rolling baseline, at least for columns used in KPIs and ML features. Schedule distribution checks weekly rather than daily to control cost.

commonMistakes.mistake: Setting a single global k-sigma threshold (e.g., k=3 for all metrics) without per-metric tuning.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Using a single default threshold is simple to configure and appears principled because k=3 is a standard statistical convention.
commonMistakes.impact: High-variance metrics (event counts that swing 50% week-to-week) produce constant false positives at k=3; low-variance metrics (null rates on a clean column) miss real anomalies that are only 2 sigma away because the stddev is tiny. Alert fatigue on the high-variance metrics causes engineers to ignore alerts from the low-variance ones too.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Tune k-sigma per metric based on backtesting against historical incidents. Use tighter thresholds (k=2-2.5) for low-variance, high-impact metrics (revenue-critical null rates, fraud feature values) and wider thresholds (k=3.5-4) for inherently high-variance metrics (user event counts, click-through rates).

comparisonSection.optionA: Static threshold (e.g., alert if row count < 100,000)
comparisonSection.optionB: Dynamic/adaptive anomaly detection (z-score on same-DOW rolling window, STL, Prophet)
comparisonSection.explanation: Static thresholds require an engineer to know the right absolute value for every metric and to update it as volumes grow or seasons shift. They produce false positives on predictable low-volume periods (weekends, holidays) and require constant maintenance. Dynamic detectors learn the expected range from history, adapt to seasonality and trend automatically, and flag deviations relative to context rather than absolute values—catching unknown-unknowns at the cost of cold-start period and sensitivity tuning.

comparisonSection.feature: Detecting distribution shift vs volume anomalies
comparisonSection.optionA: Row count / null rate anomaly detection (z-score on aggregate metrics)
comparisonSection.optionB: Distribution shift detection (PSI, KS test on full column distributions)
comparisonSection.explanation: Volume anomaly detection is cheap, fast, and catches the majority of pipeline failures (row drops, null spikes). But it is blind to changes in the shape of the distribution when total volume is stable: a price increase that shifts all order amounts upward, a change in user demographics that shifts age distributions, or a feature normalization bug that compresses the variance of a key ML feature all pass volume checks while silently corrupting analytics and model performance. Distribution shift detection (PSI, KS) is more expensive (requires computing histograms or CDFs) but essential for ML feature monitoring and catching subtle upstream changes.

comparisonSection.feature: Robustness to outliers in the history window
comparisonSection.explanation: Z-score is the most widely understood and easiest to implement but is sensitive to outliers in the reference window: a single extreme historical value inflates the standard deviation, widening bounds and causing the detector to miss subsequent real anomalies. MAD uses the median and median absolute deviation, which are not affected by a few extreme values in the history window. In practice, use z-score as a default for stable, approximately normal metrics and switch to MAD for metrics with known occasional spikes in historical data that should not widen the normal bounds.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between a static threshold and a dynamic anomaly detector for data quality?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A static threshold is a fixed rule (e.g., 'alert if row count < 100,000') that requires an engineer to know the right value in advance and update it as data volumes change. A dynamic anomaly detector learns the expected range from historical metric values and flags deviations relative to that learned baseline, adapting automatically to trends and seasonality.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Interviewers expect you to note that static rules only catch known failure modes while dynamic detectors catch unknown-unknowns. Mention the trade-off: dynamic detectors need historical data to work (cold-start problem) and require sensitivity tuning to avoid alert fatigue.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is z-score-based anomaly detection and how would you apply it to a daily row count metric?
beginnerQuestions.answer: The z-score measures how many standard deviations today's value is from the mean of a reference distribution: z = (x - mean) / std. For a daily row count, you compute the mean and standard deviation of the last N same-day-of-week row count values from history, then flag today's count as anomalous if |z| > 3.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Stress the importance of same-day-of-week grouping to handle weekly seasonality. A common mistake is using a naive 30-day rolling window that mixes weekday and weekend values, inflating variance and causing false positives every weekend.

intermediateQuestions.question: When would you choose MAD over z-score for anomaly detection on data quality metrics?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Use MAD when the historical metric series contains occasional outliers (past incidents, one-off data loads) that should not widen the normal bounds for future detection. Z-score's mean and std are sensitive to outliers: one extreme historical value inflates std, making the detector too lenient. MAD uses median and median absolute deviation, which are robust to a few extreme values in the reference window.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Give a concrete example: a row_count metric that had one known incident day with 5x the normal volume in the past 30 days will inflate the z-score std, potentially missing a real 50% drop today. MAD on the same window will not be affected by that spike.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is PSI and how do you use it to detect distribution shift in a data pipeline?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Population Stability Index (PSI) measures how much a distribution has shifted between a baseline period and a current period: PSI = sum((actual_pct_i - expected_pct_i) * ln(actual_pct_i / expected_pct_i)) over bins. PSI < 0.1 is stable, 0.1-0.2 is moderate shift, > 0.2 is significant. You compute it by binning both the baseline and current distributions on the same edges, computing per-bin fractions, and summing the PSI formula.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Mention the practical steps: derive bin edges from the combined range of both distributions to ensure comparability; add a small epsilon to avoid log(0) on empty bins; set bin edges once from the baseline and reuse them for all future current windows so comparisons are consistent over time.

advancedQuestions.question: How would you handle seasonality in anomaly detection for a data pipeline metric that shows strong weekly and monthly patterns?
advancedQuestions.answer: For weekly seasonality, group historical observations by day-of-week and compute baselines (mean, std) only over same-DOW history. For monthly patterns (e.g., month-end spikes), use STL decomposition to separate trend, weekly seasonal, and monthly seasonal components, fit the anomaly detector to the residuals after removing seasonal components, and generate bounds in residual space that are then re-added to the forecast. Prophet is a practical alternative that models both seasonalities plus holidays and generates forecast confidence intervals directly usable as anomaly bounds.
advancedQuestions.explanation: A strong answer demonstrates understanding of why naive rolling windows fail for seasonal data and describes at least one concrete method (DOW grouping, STL, or Prophet) with its trade-offs: DOW grouping is simple but only handles weekly seasonality; STL handles arbitrary seasonality but requires sufficient history; Prophet handles holidays but is more complex to operationalize at scale.

advancedQuestions.question: Design a production anomaly detection system for 500 tables with 10 metrics each (5,000 metric time series). How do you make it scalable, maintainable, and low in alert fatigue?
advancedQuestions.answer: Store all metrics in a single partitioned metrics_history table. Run detection via SQL window functions pushed to the warehouse—one query covers all 5,000 series by partitioning on (table_name, metric_name, day_of_week). Precompute and cache DOW statistics daily so detection queries are joins, not recomputations. Tier sensitivity: critical tables (k=2.5), standard tables (k=3), high-variance tables (k=3.5). Implement warm-up guards (history_count >= 8 same-DOW observations) for cold start. Route P1 anomalies to PagerDuty, P2 to Slack; suppress repeated alerts for the same (table, metric) within 4 hours. Track and review false positive rates weekly, tuning k-sigma per metric based on engineer feedback.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Interviewers look for: SQL pushdown for scale; per-metric sensitivity tiering; cold-start handling; alert routing and deduplication; and feedback-based tuning. The answer should show that the system is not just technically correct but operationally sustainable for a large-scale environment.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your anomaly detector has been running for 6 months and the on-call team has started ignoring its alerts because 'they're almost always false positives.' How do you diagnose and fix this?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Alert fatigue from false positives usually has three root causes: (1) sensitivity too high (k-sigma too low for the metric's natural variance), (2) seasonality not handled so predictable low-volume periods trigger alerts, or (3) cold-start false positives from new tables that were never filtered. Start by quantifying the false positive rate from acknowledgement data, then identify which metrics are responsible for the noise.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: First, query the anomaly results table with engineer acknowledgement labels to compute false positive rate per (table, metric)—you likely find that 3-5 high-variance or seasonal metrics are responsible for 80% of false positives. For each noisy metric: check if DOW grouping is applied (fix if not), check the k-sigma setting (raise to 3.5+ if naturally high-variance), check whether the metric has sufficient warm-up history (add cold-start guard if not). Implement alert deduplication (suppress if the same alert fired in the last 4 hours without resolution). After fixes, run a 2-week backtest to confirm the false positive rate drops below 20% before re-engaging the on-call team. Consider a feedback loop where engineers can mark alerts as false positives directly from Slack, feeding an ongoing sensitivity calibration process.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design an end-to-end anomaly detection system for a data platform with 200 production tables, daily batch pipelines, and a real-time ML serving layer that needs to detect both pipeline volume/freshness anomalies and feature distribution drift within one pipeline cycle (30 minutes).
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Architecture: (1) Post-load metric computation step in each pipeline DAG writes row counts, null rates, distinct counts, freshness lag, and p50/p95 per column to a Snowflake metrics_history table (partitioned by table_name, metric_name, partition_date). (2) Distribution histogram step writes pre-binned column histograms (JSON) to a dq_distribution_histograms table daily. (3) An anomaly detection DAG runs after each load: SQL window function query computes z-scores against 28-day same-DOW rolling statistics for all metrics; Python step runs PSI between today's and 30-day-baseline histograms for ML feature columns. (4) Results are written to a dq_anomaly_results table. (5) Alert routing step queries results, applies severity tier rules (|z| > 10 or PSI > 0.3 = P1 PagerDuty; others = P2 Slack), deduplicates within 4 hours, and sends alerts with table lineage context. (6) Grafana dashboard reads dq_anomaly_results for real-time status view.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: SQL-pushdown for detection scales to 200 tables cheaply but requires a well-maintained metrics_history table; Python distribution shift is more expensive and runs daily not on every load. Same-DOW baselines handle weekly seasonality but not monthly or holiday seasonality without additional decomposition. Tiering sensitivity by table importance reduces alert volume but means lower-tier tables may miss moderate anomalies.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: For 2,000+ tables, materialize DOW statistics incrementally (insert new row daily, never recompute full window) and partition detection queries by table_name cluster key. Switch distribution shift computation to approximate histograms using T-Digest or warehouse-native approximate percentile functions. Move alert routing to an event-driven architecture (SNS/SQS or Pub/Sub) so it decouples from the DAG execution time and does not add to the critical-path latency. Implement a catalog-driven configuration store that auto-registers new tables for monitoring when they are added to the platform, eliminating the manual onboarding step.
